gene.name: adenosine deaminase
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine and 2- deoxyadenosine. Plays an important role in purine metabolism and in adenosine homeostasis. Modulates signaling by extracellular adenosine, and so contributes indirectly to cellular signaling events. Acts as a positive regulator of T-cell coactivation, by binding DPP4. Its interaction with DPP4 regulates lymphocyte-epithelial cell adhesion. Enhances dendritic cell immunogenicity by affecting dendritic cell costimulatory molecule expression and cytokines and chemokines secretion (By similarity). Enhances CD4+ T-cell differentiation and proliferation. Acts as a positive modulator of adenosine receptors ADORA1 and ADORA2A, by enhancing their ligand affinity via conformational change. Stimulates plasminogen activation. Plays a role in male fertility. Plays a protective role in early postimplantation embryonic development (By similarity). Also responsible for the deamination of cordycepin (3'-deoxyadenosine), a fungal natural product that shows antitumor, antibacterial, antifungal, antivirus, and immune regulation properties.

gene.name: adenosine deaminase RNA specific
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) referred to as A-to-I RNA editing. This may affect gene expression and function in a number of ways that include mRNA translation by changing codons and hence the amino acid sequence of proteins since the translational machinery read the inosine as a guanosine; pre-mRNA splicing by altering splice site recognition sequences; RNA stability by changing sequences involved in nuclease recognition; genetic stability in the case of RNA virus genomes by changing sequences during viral RNA replication; and RNA structure- dependent activities such as microRNA production or targeting or protein-RNA interactions. Can edit both viral and cellular RNAs and can edit RNAs at multiple sites (hyper-editing) or at specific sites (site- specific editing). Its cellular RNA substrates include: bladder cancer- associated protein (BLCAP), neurotransmitter receptors for glutamate (GRIA2) and serotonin (HTR2C) and GABA receptor (GABRA3). Site-specific RNA editing of transcripts encoding these proteins results in amino acid substitutions which consequently alters their functional activities. Exhibits low-level editing at the GRIA2 Q/R site, but edits efficiently at the R/G site and HOTSPOT1. Its viral RNA substrates include: hepatitis C virus (HCV), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), measles virus (MV), hepatitis delta virus (HDV), and human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1). Exhibits either a proviral (HDV, MV, VSV and HIV-1) or an antiviral effect (HCV) and this can be editing-dependent (HDV and HCV), editing-independent (VSV and MV) or both (HIV-1). Impairs HCV replication via RNA editing at multiple sites. Enhances the replication of MV, VSV and HIV-1 through an editing-independent mechanism via suppression of EIF2AK2/PKR activation and function. Stimulates both the release and infectivity of HIV-1 viral particles by an editing-dependent mechanism where it associates with viral RNAs and edits adenosines in the 5'UTR and the Rev and Tat coding sequence. Can enhance viral replication of HDV via A-to-I editing at a site designated as amber/W, thereby changing an UAG amber stop codon to an UIG tryptophan (W) codon that permits synthesis of the large delta antigen (L-HDAg) which has a key role in the assembly of viral particles. However, high levels of ADAR1 inhibit HDV replication.

gene.name: adenosine deaminase RNA specific B1
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) referred to as A-to-I RNA editing. This may affect gene expression and function in a number of ways that include mRNA translation by changing codons and hence the amino acid sequence of proteins; pre-mRNA splicing by altering splice site recognition sequences; RNA stability by changing sequences involved in nuclease recognition; genetic stability in the case of RNA virus genomes by changing sequences during viral RNA replication; and RNA structure-dependent activities such as microRNA production or targeting or protein-RNA interactions. Can edit both viral and cellular RNAs and can edit RNAs at multiple sites (hyper-editing) or at specific sites (site-specific editing). Its cellular RNA substrates include: bladder cancer-associated protein (BLCAP), neurotransmitter receptors for glutamate (GRIA2 and GRIK2) and serotonin (HTR2C), GABA receptor (GABRA3) and potassium voltage-gated channel (KCNA1). Site-specific RNA editing of transcripts encoding these proteins results in amino acid substitutions which consequently alter their functional activities. Edits GRIA2 at both the Q/R and R/G sites efficiently but converts the adenosine in hotspot1 much less efficiently. Can exert a proviral effect towards human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) and enhances its replication via both an editing-dependent and editing-independent mechanism. The former involves editing of adenosines in the 5'UTR while the latter occurs via suppression of EIF2AK2/PKR activation and function. Can inhibit cell proliferation and migration and can stimulate exocytosis.

gene.name: alkaline phosphatase, biomineralization associated
gene.function: Alkaline phosphatase that metabolizes various phosphate compounds and plays a key role in skeletal mineralization and adaptive thermogenesis. Has broad substrate specificity and can hydrolyze a considerable variety of compounds: however, only a few substrates, such as diphosphate (inorganic pyrophosphate; PPi), pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) and N- phosphocreatine are natural substrates. Plays an essential role in skeletal and dental mineralization via its ability to hydrolyze extracellular diphosphate, a potent mineralization inhibitor, to phosphate: it thereby promotes hydroxyapatite crystal formation and increases inorganic phosphate concentration. Acts in a non- redundant manner with PHOSPHO1 in skeletal mineralization: while PHOSPHO1 mediates the initiation of hydroxyapatite crystallization in the matrix vesicles (MVs), ALPL/TNAP catalyzes the spread of hydroxyapatite crystallization in the extracellular matrix (By similarity). Also promotes dephosphorylation of osteopontin (SSP1), an inhibitor of hydroxyapatite crystallization in its phosphorylated state; it is however unclear whether ALPL/TNAP mediates SSP1 dephosphorylation via a direct or indirect manner (By similarity). Catalyzes dephosphorylation of PLP to pyridoxal (PL), the transportable form of vitamin B6, in order to provide a sufficient amount of PLP in the brain, an essential cofactor for enzymes catalyzing the synthesis of diverse neurotransmitters. Additionally, also able to mediate ATP degradation in a stepwise manner to adenosine, thereby regulating the availability of ligands for purinergic receptors (By similarity). Also capable of dephosphorylating microbial products, such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) as well as other phosphorylated small-molecules, such as poly-inosine:cytosine (poly I:C). Acts as a key regulator of adaptive thermogenesis as part of the futile creatine cycle: localizes to the mitochondria of thermogenic fat cells and acts by mediating hydrolysis of N-phosphocreatine to initiate a futile cycle of creatine dephosphorylation and phosphorylation (By similarity). During the futile creatine cycle, creatine and N-phosphocreatine are in a futile cycle, which dissipates the high energy charge of N-phosphocreatine as heat without performing any mechanical or chemical work (By similarity).

gene.name: complement C7
gene.function: Component of the membrane attack complex (MAC), a multiprotein complex activated by the complement cascade, which inserts into a target cell membrane and forms a pore, leading to target cell membrane rupture and cell lysis. The MAC is initiated by proteolytic cleavage of C5 into complement C5b in response to the classical, alternative, lectin and GZMK complement pathways. The complement pathways consist in a cascade of proteins that leads to phagocytosis and breakdown of pathogens and signaling that strengthens the adaptive immune system. C7 serves as a membrane anchor. During MAC assembly, associates with C5b and C6 to form the C5b-7 complex, a key lipophilic precursor of the MAC complex, which associates with the outer leaflet and reduces the energy for membrane bending.

gene.name: C-C motif chemokine receptor 5
gene.function: Receptor for a number of inflammatory CC-chemokines including CCL3/MIP-1-alpha, CCL4/MIP-1-beta and RANTES and subsequently transduces a signal by increasing the intracellular calcium ion level. May play a role in the control of granulocytic lineage proliferation or differentiation. Participates in T-lymphocyte migration to the infection site by acting as a chemotactic receptor.

gene.name: CF transmembrane conductance regulator
gene.function: Epithelial ion channel that plays an important role in the regulation of epithelial ion and water transport and fluid homeostasis. Mediates the transport of chloride ions across the cell membrane. Possesses an intrinsic ATPase activity and utilizes ATP to gate its channel; the passive flow of anions through the channel is gated by cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis by the ATP-binding domains. The ion channel is also permeable to HCO(3)(-); selectivity depends on the extracellular chloride concentration. In vitro, mediates ATP-dependent glutathione flux. Exerts its function also by modulating the activity of other ion channels and transporters. Plays an important role in airway fluid homeostasis. Contributes to the regulation of the pH and the ion content of the airway surface fluid layer and thereby plays an important role in defense against pathogens. Modulates the activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) complex, in part by regulating the cell surface expression of the ENaC complex. Inhibits the activity of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B and SCNN1G. Inhibits the activity of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1D, SCNN1B and SCNN1G, but not of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B and SCNN1G. May regulate bicarbonate secretion and salvage in epithelial cells by regulating the transporter SLC4A7. Can inhibit the chloride channel activity of ANO1. Plays a role in the chloride and bicarbonate homeostasis during sperm epididymal maturation and capacitation.

gene.name: collagen type X alpha 1 chain
gene.function: Type X collagen is a product of hypertrophic chondrocytes and has been localized to presumptive mineralization zones of hyaline cartilage.

gene.name: collagen type VII alpha 1 chain
gene.function: Stratified squamous epithelial basement membrane protein that forms anchoring fibrils which may contribute to epithelial basement membrane organization and adherence by interacting with extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins such as type IV collagen.

gene.name: dystrophin
gene.function: Anchors the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton via F- actin. Ligand for dystroglycan. Component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex which accumulates at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and at a variety of synapses in the peripheral and central nervous systems and has a structural function in stabilizing the sarcolemma. Also implicated in signaling events and synaptic transmission.

gene.name: eukaryotic translation termination factor 1
gene.function: Component of the eRF1-eRF3-GTP ternary complex, a ternary complex that mediates translation termination in response to the termination codons. The eRF1-eRF3-GTP complex binds to a stop codon in the ribosomal A-site. ETF1/ERF1 is responsible for stop codon recognition and inducing hydrolysis of peptidyl-tRNA. Following GTP hydrolysis, eRF3 (GSPT1/ERF3A or GSPT2/ERF3B) dissociates, permitting ETF1/eRF1 to accommodate fully in the A-site and mediate hydrolysis of peptidyl-tRNA. Component of the transient SURF complex which recruits UPF1 to stalled ribosomes in the context of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of mRNAs containing premature stop codons. Required for SHFL-mediated translation termination which inhibits programmed ribosomal frameshifting (-1PRF) of mRNA from viruses and cellular genes.

gene.name: forkhead box P3
gene.function: Transcriptional regulator which is crucial for the development and inhibitory function of regulatory T-cells (Treg). Plays an essential role in maintaining homeostasis of the immune system by allowing the acquisition of full suppressive function and stability of the Treg lineage, and by directly modulating the expansion and function of conventional T-cells. Can act either as a transcriptional repressor or a transcriptional activator depending on its interactions with other transcription factors, histone acetylases and deacetylases. The suppressive activity of Treg involves the coordinate activation of many genes, including CTLA4 and TNFRSF18 by FOXP3 along with repression of genes encoding cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL2) and interferon-gamma (IFNG). Inhibits cytokine production and T-cell effector function by repressing the activity of two key transcription factors, RELA and NFATC2. Mediates transcriptional repression of IL2 via its association with histone acetylase KAT5 and histone deacetylase HDAC7. Can activate the expression of TNFRSF18, IL2RA and CTLA4 and repress the expression of IL2 and IFNG via its association with transcription factor RUNX1. Inhibits the differentiation of IL17 producing helper T-cells (Th17) by antagonizing RORC function, leading to down-regulation of IL17 expression, favoring Treg development. Inhibits the transcriptional activator activity of RORA. Can repress the expression of IL2 and IFNG via its association with transcription factor IKZF4 (By similarity).

gene.name: galactosamine (N-acetyl)-6-sulfatase
gene.function: Lysosomal enzyme that hydrolyzes sulfate groups from glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), keratan sulfate (KS) and chondroitin-6- sulfate (C6S). .

gene.name: G1 to S phase transition 1
gene.function: GTPase component of the eRF1-eRF3-GTP ternary complex, a ternary complex that mediates translation termination in response to the termination codons UAA, UAG and UGA. GSPT1/ERF3A mediates ETF1/ERF1 delivery to stop codons: The eRF1-eRF3-GTP complex binds to a stop codon in the ribosomal A-site. GTP hydrolysis by GSPT1/ERF3A induces a conformational change that leads to its dissociation, permitting ETF1/ERF1 to accommodate fully in the A-site. Component of the transient SURF complex which recruits UPF1 to stalled ribosomes in the context of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of mRNAs containing premature stop codons. Required for SHFL-mediated translation termination which inhibits programmed ribosomal frameshifting (-1PRF) of mRNA from viruses and cellular genes.

gene.name: G1 to S phase transition 2
gene.function: GTPase component of the eRF1-eRF3-GTP ternary complex, a ternary complex that mediates translation termination in response to the termination codons UAA, UAG and UGA. GSPT2/ERF3B mediates ETF1/ERF1 delivery to stop codons: The eRF1-eRF3-GTP complex binds to a stop codon in the ribosomal A-site. GTP hydrolysis by GSPT2/ERF3B induces a conformational change that leads to its dissociation, permitting ETF1/ERF1 to accommodate fully in the A-site. Component of the transient SURF complex which recruits UPF1 to stalled ribosomes in the context of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of mRNAs containing premature stop codons.

gene.name: glucuronidase beta
gene.function: Plays an important role in the degradation of dermatan and keratan sulfates.

gene.name: iduronate 2-sulfatase
gene.function: Lysosomal enzyme involved in the degradation pathway of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate.

gene.name: alpha-L-iduronidase
gene.function: Lysosomal hydrolase responsible for the degradation of the glycosaminoglycans heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. .

gene.name: Indian hedgehog signaling molecule
gene.function: Precursor of indian hedgehog, a morphogen that activates the smoothened signaling pathway, and which is essential for bone and cartilage development (By similarity). The C- terminal part of the precursor displays an autoproteolysis and a cholesterol transferase activity, resulting (1) in the cleavage of the full-length protein into two parts, indian hedgehog protein N-product and C-product and (2) covalent attachment of a cholesterol moiety to the C-terminus of the newly generated N-product (By similarity). Both autoproteolysis and a cholesterol transferase activities occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (By similarity). Following additional lipidation, N-product acts as a morphogen, while C-product is degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum (By similarity).

gene.name: mannose-6-phosphate receptor, cation dependent
gene.function: Transport of phosphorylated lysosomal enzymes from the Golgi complex and the cell surface to lysosomes. Lysosomal enzymes bearing phosphomannosyl residues bind specifically to mannose-6-phosphate receptors in the Golgi apparatus and the resulting receptor-ligand complex is transported to an acidic prelyosomal compartment where the low pH mediates the dissociation of the complex.

gene.name: natriuretic peptide C
gene.function: Hormone which plays a role in endochondral ossification through regulation of cartilaginous growth plate chondrocytes proliferation and differentiation (By similarity). May also be vasoactive and natriuretic. Acts by specifically binding and stimulating NPR2 to produce cGMP. Binds the clearance receptor NPR3.

gene.name: protein kinase cAMP-dependent type I regulatory subunit alpha
gene.function: Regulatory subunit of the cAMP-dependent protein kinases involved in cAMP signaling in cells.

gene.name: retinoid isomerohydrolase RPE65
gene.function: Critical isomerohydrolase in the retinoid cycle involved in regeneration of 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rod and cone opsins. Catalyzes the cleavage and isomerization of all-trans-retinyl fatty acid esters to 11-cis-retinol which is further oxidized by 11-cis retinol dehydrogenase to 11-cis-retinal for use as visual chromophore. Essential for the production of 11-cis retinal for both rod and cone photoreceptors. Also capable of catalyzing the isomerization of lutein to meso-zeaxanthin an eye- specific carotenoid. The soluble form binds vitamin A (all-trans-retinol), making it available for LRAT processing to all- trans-retinyl ester. The membrane form, palmitoylated by LRAT, binds all-trans-retinyl esters, making them available for IMH (isomerohydrolase) processing to all-cis-retinol. The soluble form is regenerated by transferring its palmitoyl groups onto 11-cis-retinol, a reaction catalyzed by LRAT (By similarity).

gene.name: RUNX family transcription factor 2
gene.function: Transcription factor involved in osteoblastic differentiation and skeletal morphogenesis. Essential for the maturation of osteoblasts and both intramembranous and endochondral ossification. CBF binds to the core site, 5'-PYGPYGGT-3', of a number of enhancers and promoters, including murine leukemia virus, polyomavirus enhancer, T- cell receptor enhancers, osteocalcin, osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, alpha 1(I) collagen, LCK, IL-3 and GM-CSF promoters. In osteoblasts, supports transcription activation: synergizes with SPEN/MINT to enhance FGFR2-mediated activation of the osteocalcin FGF-responsive element (OCFRE) (By similarity). Inhibits KAT6B-dependent transcriptional activation.

gene.name: N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase
gene.function: Catalyzes a step in lysosomal heparan sulfate degradation.

gene.name: structural maintenance of chromosomes flexible hinge domain containing 1
gene.function: Non-canonical member of the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) protein family that plays a key role in epigenetic silencing by regulating chromatin architecture (By similarity). Promotes heterochromatin formation in both autosomes and chromosome X, probably by mediating the merge of chromatin compartments (By similarity). Plays a key role in chromosome X inactivation in females by promoting the spreading of heterochromatin. Recruited to inactivated chromosome X by Xist RNA and acts by mediating the merge of chromatin compartments: promotes random chromatin interactions that span the boundaries of existing structures, leading to create a compartment-less architecture typical of inactivated chromosome X (By similarity). Required to facilitate Xist RNA spreading (By similarity). Also required for silencing of a subset of clustered autosomal loci in somatic cells, such as the DUX4 locus. Has ATPase activity; may participate in structural manipulation of chromatin in an ATP-dependent manner as part of its role in gene expression regulation. Also plays a role in DNA repair: localizes to sites of DNA double-strand breaks in response to DNA damage to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Acts by promoting non- homologous end joining (NHEJ) and inhibiting homologous recombination (HR) repair.

gene.name: smoothened, frizzled class receptor
gene.function: G protein-coupled receptor, which transduces the smoothened signaling pathway. Activated by cholesterol in response to hedgehog (DHH, IHH or SHH) morphogens. In absence of hedgehog, SMO is inactivated by patched protein (PTCH1 or PTCH2), which prevents SMO access to cholesterol. In response to hedgehog-binding to pathched, inhibition is relieved, promoting SMO translocation to primary cilium and activation by cholesterol: cholesterol causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via G protein G(i), mediating inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity and decreassed production of cAMP. Decreased cAMP levels then inhibit protein kinase A (PKA) and promote release of GLI (GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3) transcription factors, which activate expression of target genes. Active SMO also directly inhibits PKA by sequestering its catalytic subunit, PRKACA, at the cell membrane, preventing PRKACA-mediated phosphorylation and subsequent processing of GLI transcription factors. Active SMO also promotes the removal of GPR161, a key inhibitor of the smoothened signaling pathway, from primary cilia (By similarity).

gene.name: transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily V member 4
gene.function: Non-selective calcium permeant cation channel involved in osmotic sensitivity and mechanosensitivity. Activation by exposure to hypotonicity within the physiological range exhibits an outward rectification. Also activated by heat, low pH, citrate and phorbol esters. Increase of intracellular Ca(2+) potentiates currents. Channel activity seems to be regulated by a calmodulin-dependent mechanism with a negative feedback mechanism. Promotes cell-cell junction formation in skin keratinocytes and plays an important role in the formation and/or maintenance of functional intercellular barriers (By similarity). Acts as a regulator of intracellular Ca(2+) in synoviocytes. Plays an obligatory role as a molecular component in the nonselective cation channel activation induced by 4-alpha-phorbol 12,13-didecanoate and hypotonic stimulation in synoviocytes and also regulates production of IL-8. Together with PKD2, forms mechano- and thermosensitive channels in cilium. Negatively regulates expression of PPARGC1A, UCP1, oxidative metabolism and respiration in adipocytes (By similarity). Regulates expression of chemokines and cytokines related to pro-inflammatory pathway in adipocytes (By similarity). Together with AQP5, controls regulatory volume decrease in salivary epithelial cells (By similarity). Required for normal development and maintenance of bone and cartilage. In its inactive state, may sequester DDX3X at the plasma membrane. When activated, the interaction between both proteins is affected and DDX3X relocalizes to the nucleus. In neurons of the central nervous system, could play a role in triggering voluntary water intake in response to increased sodium concentration in body fluid (By similarity).

gene.name: usherin
gene.function: Involved in hearing and vision as member of the USH2 complex. In the inner ear, required for the maintenance of the hair bundle ankle formation, which connects growing stereocilia in developing cochlear hair cells. In retina photoreceptors, the USH2 complex is required for the maintenance of periciliary membrane complex that seems to play a role in regulating intracellular protein transport. .

phenotype.definition: An increased white blood cell count in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Compression of the spinal cord in the cervical region, generally manifested by paresthesias and numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, abnormalities of coordination, and neck pain or stiffness.

Absence of fine and sharp appearance of brows, nose, lips, mouth, and chin, usually because of rounded and heavy features or thickened skin with or without thickening of subcutaneous and bony tissues.
Abnormal cognition is characterized by deficits in thinking, reasoning, or remembering.
A reduction of corneal clarity.

Frequently experiencing feelings of being down, miserable, and/or hopeless; struggling to recover from these moods; having a pessimistic outlook on the future; feeling a pervasive sense of shame; having a low self-worth; experiencing thoughts of suicide and engaging in suicidal behavior.
Impaired ability to eat related to problems gathering food and getting ready to suck, chew, or swallow it.
Delay of conduction through the atrioventricular node, which is manifested as prolongation of the PR interval in the electrocardiogram (EKG). All atrial impulses reach the ventricles.
A deficiency or slowing down of growth pre- and postnatally.
Abnormally increased size of the liver.
Simultaneous enlargement of the liver and spleen.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the hip.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the hip.

Hydrocephalus is an active distension of the ventricular system of the brain resulting from inadequate passage of CSF from its point of production within the cerebral ventricles to its point of absorption into the systemic circulation.
phenotype.lay: Too much cerebrospinal fluid in the brain

phenotype.definition: Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist.

An abnormally increased head circumference in a growing child. Head circumference is measured with a nonelastic tape and comprises the distance from above the eyebrows and ears and around the back of the head. The measured HC is then plotted on an appropriate growth chart.
Protrusion of the contents of the abdominal cavity through the inguinal canal.

A limitation in the passive range of motion of a joint resulting from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues owing to structural changes of non-bony tissues, such as muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules or skin. A contracture prevents movement of the associated body part.

nodes.label: Joint stiffness
names: restriction of joint range of motion

phenotype.definition: Joint stiffness is a perceived sensation of tightness in a joint or joints when attempting to move them after a period of inactivity. Joint stiffness typically subsides over time.
Exaggerated anterior convexity of the thoracic vertebral column.
Inability to walk in a person who previous had the ability to walk.
Excessive amounts of mucopolysaccharide in the urine.

Myelopathy is an descriptive term, referring to pathology leading to a neurologic deficit related to the spinal cord. The clinical diagnosis of myelopathy requires a detailed history and physical examination to define the clinical syndrome. Neuroimaging is indicated in most instances of new-onset myelopathy. It is indicated also when the worsening of a myelopathy is unexplained.
Progressive loss of neural cells and tissue.
Activation of the brain's innate immune system in response to an inflammatory challenge and is characterized by a host of cellular and molecular changes within the brain.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea is a condition characterized by the obstruction of the airway and pauses in breathing during sleep, which occur multiple times throughout the night. It is related to the relaxation of muscle tone that typically happens during sleep, leading to a partial collapse of the soft tissues in the airway and causing airflow obstruction.

Osteopenia is a term to define bone density that is not normal but also not as low as osteoporosis. By definition from the World Health Organization osteopenia is defined by bone densitometry as a T score -1 to -2.5.
Inflammation or infection of the middle ear.
An increased susceptibility to respiratory infections as manifested by a history of recurrent respiratory infections.
Peripheral neuropathy affecting the sensory nerves.
phenotype.lay: Damage to nerves that sense feeling

phenotype.definition: A height below that which is expected according to age and gender norms. Although there is no universally accepted definition of short stature, many refer to "short stature" as height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender (or below the 3rd percentile for age and gender dependent norms).
A general term describing features characterized by abnormal development of bones and connective tissues.

An intermittent cessation of airflow at the mouth and nose during sleep is known as sleep apnea. Apneas that last at least 10 seconds are considered significant, but individuals with sleep apnea may experience apneas lasting from 20 seconds up to 2 or 3 minutes. Patients may have up to 15 events per hour of sleep.
Hyperconvexity of the thoracolumbar spine producing a rounded or humped appearance.
Increased resistance to the passage of air in the upper airway.

Visual impairment (or vision impairment) is vision loss (of a person) to such a degree as to qualify as an additional support need through a significant limitation of visual capability resulting from either disease, trauma, or congenital or degenerative conditions that cannot be corrected by conventional means, such as refractive correction, medication, or surgery.

papers.title: Early treatment with laronidase improves clinical outcomes in patients with attenuated MPS I: a retrospective case series analysis of nine sibships.
papers.summary: This retrospective sibling case series reports that early, pre-symptomatic initiation of laronidase enzyme replacement therapy in attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis type I was associated with improved or stabilized somatic manifestations, less progression of cardiac, musculoskeletal, motor, and cognitive symptoms, and better height outcomes than later treatment. The findings do not demonstrate improved growth consistently or prevention of corneal clouding, and the retrospective design, missing data, subjective assessments, variable compliance, and possible phenotypic differences limit causal conclusions.
papers.why: The sibling case series provides clinical outcome data suggesting that early laronidase treatment can stabilize or prevent severe somatic manifestations in attenuated MPS I.

papers.title: Immune tolerance induction for laronidase treatment in mucopolysaccharidosis I.
papers.summary: In a small, prematurely terminated open-label Phase 2 study, prophylactic cyclosporine plus azathioprine before laronidase did not establish the prespecified immune-tolerance endpoint in Cohort 1, while one evaluable patient in Cohort 2 met it. Laronidase reduced urinary glycosaminoglycan excretion in all treated patients, but none reached normal levels, and lower anti-laronidase antibody titers were associated with greater reductions; the small sample, premature discontinuation, and lack of statistical analysis limit conclusions.
papers.why: This trial provides tested immunosuppression and laronidase-desensitization strategies plus efficacy and immunogenicity endpoints for managing anti-drug antibodies in severe MPS I.

papers.title: Genetically corrected autologous stem cells engraft, but host immune responses limit their utility in canine alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency.
papers.summary: Genetically corrected autologous hematopoietic cells expressed enzymatically active alpha-L-iduronidase and engrafted long term in dogs with alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, but enzyme and transcript expression were not detectable in vivo and no clinical improvement occurred. Posttransplant cyclosporine A dampened immune responses without restoring detectable alpha-L-iduronidase activity.
papers.why: The canine study directly tests genetically corrected autologous stem-cell therapy in alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency and identifies immune and expression barriers.

papers.title: Enzyme replacement therapy and/or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at diagnosis in patients with mucopolysaccharidosis type I: results of a European consensus procedure.
papers.summary: This consensus guideline recommends hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for patients with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I-H diagnosed before age 2.5 years and recommends laronidase enzyme replacement therapy from diagnosis for all symptomatic MPS I patients. Laronidase improves non-neurological and somatic disease but does not prevent neurocognitive decline because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier sufficiently, while early HSCT may preserve cognition but carries procedure-related morbidity and mortality.
papers.why: Provides consensus-based disease-specific recommendations for selecting and timing ERT and HSCT in MPS I.

papers.title: Efficient in vitro and in vivo RNA editing via recruitment of endogenous ADARs using circular guide RNAs.
papers.summary: The paper shows that AAV8-delivered circular ADAR-recruiting guide RNAs can recruit endogenous ADAR1 to correct the IDUA-W392X premature stop codon in a mouse model of MPS I-H. In treated mice, this produced 7–17% stop-codon correction and approximately 33% less lysosomal glycosaminoglycan accumulation over two weeks, indicating partial restoration of alpha-L-iduronidase activity.
papers.why: Demonstrates durable programmable RNA editing in vivo, including correction of an IDUA nonsense mutation in a mouse model of Hurler syndrome.

papers.title: Neuropathology in mouse models of mucopolysaccharidosis type I, IIIA and IIIB.
papers.summary: In Idua knockout mice modeling mucopolysaccharidosis type I, the paper quantifies progressive neuropathology involving lysosomal and GM2 storage, altered heparan sulphate, neuroinflammation, synaptic disorganisation, and dystrophic axons between 4 and 9 months of age. It also establishes neuropathological outcome measures and assays for evaluating treatment strategies, while cortical thickness, overall neuronal number, and synaptophysin staining remain largely unchanged.
papers.why: Characterizes disease progression and measurable neuropathological biomarkers in MPS I mouse models using histological, molecular, and imaging assays.

papers.title: Outcomes of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for Hurler's syndrome in Europe: a risk factor analysis for graft failure.
papers.summary: In a European retrospective cohort of 146 patients with Hurler syndrome, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation achieved 85% survival and 56% alive-and-engrafted outcomes after a first transplant, but graft failure remained common. T-cell depletion and reduced-intensity conditioning were associated with graft failure, whereas busulfan targeting and cord blood favored sustained engraftment; cord blood was particularly associated with full donor chimerism and normal leukocyte enzyme levels.
papers.why: Identifies transplant conditioning and graft-source factors associated with graft failure and sustained engraftment in Hurler syndrome.

papers.title: Mucopolysaccharidosis I, II, and VI: Brief review and guidelines for treatment.
papers.summary: This review describes MPS I as an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by deficient α-L-iduronidase and associated with glycosaminoglycan accumulation and multisystemic manifestations. It reports that intravenous laronidase improves several somatic and functional outcomes, while hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can alter severe disease course, particularly when performed early, although neither approach corrects every manifestation.
papers.why: The guideline combines clinical and trial experience for treating more than 200 MPS patients and explicitly summarizes ERT use, monitoring, and management in MPS I.

papers.title: Neurocognitive and somatic stabilization in pediatric patients with severe Mucopolysaccharidosis Type I after 52 weeks of intravenous brain-penetrating insulin receptor antibody-iduronidase fusion protein (valanafusp alpha): an open label phase 1-2 trial.
papers.summary: In an open-label phase 1-2 trial, weekly intravenous valanafusp alpha for 52 weeks was generally safe and was associated with stabilization of cognitive function and total cortical grey-matter volume in 11 pediatric patients with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I, without a significant cognitive improvement. Somatic measures also stabilized or improved, including urinary glycosaminoglycans, liver and spleen volumes, and shoulder range of motion, while infusion reactions, dose-associated transient hypoglycemia, and unchanged cerebrospinal-fluid glycosaminoglycans were observed.
papers.why: Reports a phase 1-2 trial showing stabilization of cognitive, brain, and somatic outcomes with a blood-brain-barrier-penetrating IDUA fusion protein.

papers.title: Human genome-edited hematopoietic stem cells phenotypically correct Mucopolysaccharidosis type I.
papers.summary: The study shows that human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells genome-edited to express high levels of IDUA from the CCR5 safe-harbor locus can cross-correct patient-derived MPSI fibroblasts and partially improve biochemical, skeletal, behavioral, and neuroinflammatory manifestations after transplantation into a new NSG-IDUAX/X mouse model. The approach preserved long-term repopulation and multilineage potential, but edited cells engrafted approximately fivefold less efficiently and did not normalize brain GAG accumulation or all behavioral abnormalities.
papers.why: Genome-edited autologous hematopoietic cells produced supraphysiological IDUA and improved biochemical and phenotypic abnormalities in an MPS I mouse model.

papers.title: Self-inactivating, all-in-one AAV vectors for precision Cas9 genome editing via homology-directed repair in vivo.
papers.summary: Single-vector rAAV platforms containing Nme2Cas9, an Idua-targeting sgRNA, and a 272-bp HDR donor corrected the IduaW392X allele in neonatal MPS-I mice. The vectors increased hepatic IDUA activity to 2.3–3.0% of wild type, reduced hepatic glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and produced limited but measurable HDR, although self-elimination was partial and absolute editing efficiency remained low.
papers.why: A compact self-inactivating AAV platform corrected the disease allele through HDR and demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in an MPS I mouse model.

papers.title: Toxicology Study of Intra-Cisterna Magna Adeno-Associated Virus 9 Expressing Human Alpha-L-Iduronidase in Rhesus Macaques.
papers.summary: Suboccipital, intra-cisterna magna delivery of an AAV9 vector expressing human IDUA was well tolerated procedurally in 22 rhesus macaques, but caused dose-dependent cerebrospinal-fluid pleocytosis and asymptomatic sensory-neuron degeneration with dorsal axonopathy. The findings support clinical development of the delivery approach while indicating a need to monitor sensory toxicity closely.
papers.why: Provides preclinical safety and biodistribution data supporting intrathecal AAV9-IDUA gene therapy for Hurler syndrome and identifies sensory-neuron toxicity risk.

papers.title: The prevalence of and survival in Mucopolysaccharidosis I: Hurler, Hurler-Scheie and Scheie syndromes in the UK.
papers.summary: This UK retrospective registry study estimates the birth prevalence of mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I) at 1.07 per 100,000 live births and median survival at 11.6 years, with substantially poorer survival in Hurler syndrome. It identifies bone marrow transplantation and alpha-L-iduronidase enzyme replacement as treatment approaches, but the observational data could not definitively quantify their effects on survival.
papers.why: Provides long-term prevalence, survival, and treatment-associated outcome data useful for MPS I natural-history studies and trial planning.

papers.title: Effect of small molecule eRF3 degraders on premature termination codon readthrough.
papers.summary: In IDUA p.W402X/W402X Hurler syndrome fibroblasts, the eRF3 degrader CC-90009 combined with G418 increased full-length IDUA readthrough and restored α-L-iduronidase activity to more than 3% of the unaffected-cell reference, whereas either treatment alone produced negligible activity. The combination depleted eRF3a, eRF3b, and eRF1 and appears to promote readthrough through reduced translation termination and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, but the evidence is in vitro and clinical benefit was not tested.
papers.why: Shows that CC-90009 enhances aminoglycoside-mediated readthrough of IDUA nonsense mutations in MPS I patient-derived cells while being less toxic than CC-885.

papers.title: ZFN-Mediated In Vivo Genome Editing Corrects Murine Hurler Syndrome.
papers.summary: The study demonstrates that a single intravenous administration of AAV2/8 vectors encoding ZFNs targeting the mouse albumin locus and a human IDUA donor construct inserts hIDUA into hepatocytes, produces sustained circulating IDUA, and reduces peripheral GAG accumulation and neurobehavioral deficits in the murine Hurler syndrome model. Brain biochemical correction was limited: dermatan sulfate decreased significantly only in male mice, while heparan sulfate did not decrease, and the mechanism of cognitive benefit remains unclear.
papers.why: The study demonstrates sustained hepatic IDUA expression, systemic enzyme delivery, reduced glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and prevention of neurobehavioral deficits in mice.

papers.title: First-in-human in vivo genome editing via AAV-zinc-finger nucleases for mucopolysaccharidosis I/II and hemophilia B.
papers.summary: In a first-in-human phase 1/2 study, one-time intravenous SB-318 ZFN in vivo editing was well tolerated in three people with MPS I and produced low-level hepatic albumin-IDUA fusion transcripts in one subject. Leukocyte iduronidase activity increased transiently, but no sustained circulating enzyme expression, consistent urinary GAG response, or clinically significant disease-progression benefit was demonstrated.
papers.why: Reports first-in-human in vivo AAV-ZFN editing in MPS I with initial evidence of liver editing and transient leukocyte IDUA increases, providing directly transferable clinical and biomarker data.

papers.title: Implementation of Second-Tier Tests in Newborn Screening for Lysosomal Disorders in North Eastern Italy.
papers.summary: The paper reports a North Eastern Italy newborn-screening program in which 112,446 newborns were screened for mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I) using a multiplexed tandem mass spectrometry assay for reduced IDUA activity. Two newborns were confirmed with MPS I, both with elevated urinary and dried-blood-spot glycosaminoglycans, while pseudodeficiency alleles and benign variants produced false-positive or low-activity results; the study therefore supports dried-blood-spot GAG measurement as a second-tier test.
papers.why: Large-scale newborn screening data show that first-tier MS/MS followed by second-tier testing rapidly diagnoses MPS I while substantially reducing false positives.

papers.title: Early disease progression of Hurler syndrome.
papers.summary: This retrospective observational study characterizes the early natural history of severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) in 55 children, showing that 98.2% had clinical signs by six months while gross motor development was the earliest strongly affected developmental domain. It also describes current treatment and diagnostic limitations and identifies frequent early manifestations that may warrant prognostic evaluation in infants identified by newborn screening.
papers.why: The 55-patient natural-history study provides prospective clinical endpoints and timing data that can inform prognosis, early treatment decisions, and treatment evaluation in Hurler syndrome.

papers.title: Long-term outcomes of systemic therapies for Hurler syndrome: an international multicenter comparison.
papers.summary: This observational multicenter study compared long-term outcomes of laronidase enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), and no systemic therapy in patients with Hurler syndrome, the severe form of mucopolysaccharidosis type I. ERT improved survival relative to no systemic therapy and reduced disease burden, but HCT produced superior survival and lower cumulative incidence of hydrocephalus and cervical spinal cord compression than ERT monotherapy.
papers.why: This multicenter study directly compares long-term ERT and HCT outcomes in Hurler syndrome and quantifies survival, hydrocephalus, spinal cord compression, and neurologic progression.

papers.title: In utero adenine base editing corrects multi-organ pathology in a lethal lysosomal storage disease.
papers.summary: In utero, dual split-AAV9 delivery of ABEmax corrected the Idua W392X mutation in the Idua-W392X mouse model of MPS-IH, producing durable IDUA restoration, reduced GAG accumulation, improved survival, and amelioration of cardiac and musculoskeletal disease. Brain editing and neurological correction were limited, and postnatal treatment produced partial biochemical and cardiac benefit.
papers.why: The MPS-IH mouse study directly demonstrates in utero correction of Idua W392X with improved survival and metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cardiac pathology.

papers.title: Insights into mucopolysaccharidosis I from the structure and action of α-L-iduronidase.
papers.summary: The paper determined apo- and inhibitor-bound structures of human IDUA and identified a high-mannose N-glycan at Asn372 that interacts with substrate analogues and is required for strong enzymatic activity. Structural and biochemical analysis of the disease-relevant Pro533Arg mutation showed reduced catalytic activity and thermodynamic stability, providing a basis for genotype–phenotype interpretation and future pharmacological-chaperone design for MPS I.
papers.why: The study provides experimentally validated IDUA production, structural, biochemical, and mutational-analysis methods directly applicable to MPS I enzyme research.

papers.title: Musculoskeletal manifestations in mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 19 Hurler syndrome patients, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation stabilized or improved joint mobility, odontoid hypoplasia, and craniocervical junction dimensions in many patients, but shoulder impairment and several skeletal deformities remained or progressed. The results support multidisciplinary orthopedic surveillance and selected surgical interventions, while the authors identify anti-inflammatory approaches as promising but untested strategies.
papers.why: This longitudinal study evaluates HSCT and detailed musculoskeletal outcomes in Hurler syndrome, identifying persistent complications and useful clinical endpoints.

papers.title: 12 year follow up of enzyme-replacement therapy in two siblings with attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis I: the important role of early treatment.
papers.summary: This 12-year sibling case report suggests that early initiation of laronidase enzyme-replacement therapy in attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis type I can substantially improve clinical and biochemical outcomes compared with treatment begun after disease manifestations were established. Benefits were most apparent for prevention or improvement of facial, growth, organomegaly, joint, skeletal, and cardiac manifestations, while established abnormalities such as dysostosis multiplex, corneal clouding, and joint contractures were not reversed.
papers.why: This 12-year same-disease case series provides longitudinal evidence that early laronidase treatment substantially improves attenuated MPS I outcomes.

papers.title: Biochemical and molecular analysis in mucopolysaccharidoses: what a paediatrician must know.
papers.summary: This review describes the biochemical and molecular basis of mucopolysaccharidoses and emphasizes standardized laboratory diagnosis. For mucopolysaccharidosis type 1, it identifies IDUA deficiency, accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, enzymatic pseudodeficiency as a diagnostic limitation, and a diagnostic strategy combining enzyme activity, urinary GAG analysis, and molecular testing.
papers.why: This paper provides a concrete laboratory workflow for MPS diagnosis, including urinary GAG measurement, enzyme assays and molecular testing applicable to MPS I.

papers.title: Long term disease burden post-transplantation: three decades of observations in 25 Hurler patients successfully treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).
papers.summary: In 25 patients with Hurler syndrome who survived at least 1 year after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, long-term follow-up showed improved survival but persistent progression of skeletal, ocular, cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, and psychiatric disease. Enzyme replacement therapy normalized biochemical measures in a few patients with low or variable chimerism but did not improve forced vital capacity relative to the rest of the cohort.
papers.why: The paper provides long-term outcome data from 25 Hurler patients successfully treated with HSCT, documenting treatment durability, survival, residual disease, and late neuropsychiatric outcomes.

papers.title: Evaluation of Multiple Methods for Quantification of Glycosaminoglycan Biomarkers in Newborn Dried Blood Spots from Patients with Severe and Attenuated Mucopolysaccharidosis-I.
papers.summary: In 15 newborns with MPS-I and 30 random newborn controls, four mass-spectrometry methods quantified glycosaminoglycan-derived biomarkers in dried blood spots. The endogenous disaccharide biomarker UA-HNAc(1S) provided the strongest disease-to-control discrimination and was elevated in both severe and attenuated MPS-I, supporting its use as a second-tier newborn-screening assay to reduce false-positive results after low IDUA activity.
papers.why: All four dried-blood-spot GAG assays separated MPS I patients from newborn reference samples, with the endogenous disaccharide method providing the largest differential.

papers.title: Improved reagents for newborn screening of mucopolysaccharidosis types I, II, and VI by tandem mass spectrometry.
papers.summary: The paper develops a bisamide-containing MPS-I substrate and deuterated internal standard for tandem mass spectrometry measurement of α-l-iduronidase activity in dried blood spots. The new assay increased product signal 3.4-fold and blood-to-background response 5.6-fold over the original reagent, while distinguishing one affected child from 15 newborns with a 40-fold normal-to-affected activity ratio, although large-scale clinical performance was not yet established.
papers.why: The newly synthesized substrates produced the most sensitive reported dried-blood-spot assays for IDUA, I2S, and GNS and are scalable for multiplex newborn screening.

papers.title: Utilizing AAV-mediated LEAPER 2.0 for programmable RNA editing in non-human primates and nonsense mutation correction in humanized Hurler syndrome mice.
papers.summary: AAV-delivered LEAPER 2.0 circular ADAR-recruiting RNAs produced targeted RNA editing in non-human primates without detectable toxicity or perturbation of endogenous ADAR activity. In IDUA-W402X Hurler syndrome fibroblasts and a humanized mouse model, the optimized circ-arRNA corrected the premature stop codon, restored α-L-iduronidase activity, reduced glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and improved liver pathology.
papers.why: The study demonstrates therapeutic AAV RNA editing that corrects a pathogenic IDUA stop codon and restores enzyme function in multiple organs in a humanized Hurler mouse model.

papers.title: Treatment of hip dysplasia in patients with mucopolysaccharidosis type I after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: results of an international consensus procedure.
papers.summary: This review and modified Delphi consensus study concludes that hip dysplasia remains common and progressive in most patients with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) despite successful hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It recommends early multidisciplinary assessment, serial pelvic radiography, and consideration of corrective hip surgery, while emphasizing that surgery efficacy and long-term outcomes remain unproven and that pain, function, and quality of life should guide individual decisions.
papers.why: An international consensus procedure using case review and expert panels produced MPS I-H-specific management recommendations for treating hip dysplasia after HSCT.

papers.title: An algorithm to predict phenotypic severity in mucopolysaccharidosis type I in the first month of life.
papers.summary: The study developed and internally validated a three-step algorithm combining IDUA mutation analysis, residual IDUA activity in cultured skin fibroblasts, and early clinical signs to distinguish Hurler MPS I from attenuated phenotypes during the first month of life. In 30 patients, the complete algorithm achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity in this cohort, although external validation is required and residual IDUA activity alone could not resolve the intermediate range.
papers.why: The validated cohort algorithm integrates genotype, fibroblast enzyme activity, and early clinical features to distinguish severe Hurler disease and guide timely selection of HSCT or enzyme replacement therapy.

papers.title: Programmable DNA pyrimidine base editing via engineered uracil-DNA glycosylase.
papers.summary: The paper engineers a Deinococcus radiodurans UNG-based thymine base editor (TBE) that directly converts thymine without a deaminase and shows low cellular toxicity and limited detectable off-target editing. In IDUAW402X patient-derived Hurler syndrome cells, TBE corrected approximately 25% of targeted edits and significantly restored IDUA catalytic activity, providing an in vitro gene-correction strategy rather than clinical evidence of efficacy.
papers.why: The engineered base editor directly restores IDUA activity in Hurler patient-derived cells, providing a mutation-specific gene-correction method with demonstrated cellular efficacy.

papers.title: Light and Shadows in Newborn Screening for Lysosomal Storage Disorders: Eight Years of Experience in Northeast Italy.
papers.summary: The paper reports an eight-year newborn-screening program in which low dried-blood-spot IDUA activity was used to identify mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I), with urinary or DBS glycosaminoglycan quantification as a second-tier test. Four affected newborns were confirmed and treated promptly with laronidase enzyme-replacement therapy, with severe Hurler cases also receiving allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; the second-tier GAG test substantially reduced false-positive recalls, but pseudodeficiency variants and variants of uncertain significance remained important limitations.
papers.why: An eight-year program screened approximately 250,000 newborns, confirmed MPS I cases, and initiated early treatment, demonstrating the feasibility and diagnostic performance of the proposed screening workflow.

papers.title: Phenotype prediction for mucopolysaccharidosis type I by in silico analysis.
papers.summary: The paper combines seven computational predictors with IDUA structural and untranslated-region analyses to prioritize functional variants and infer phenotype severity in mucopolysaccharidosis type I. Its SAAMP algorithm classified known IDUA variants with 94% sensitivity and 80% specificity at a 0.43 pathogenicity cutoff, but the authors require biochemical and/or clinical confirmation and note limited sensitivity for phenotype-severity prediction.
papers.why: The study developed and evaluated an in silico workflow for predicting functional and phenotypic effects of IDUA variants with reported sensitivity and specificity.

papers.title: Intrathecal enzyme replacement therapy reverses cognitive decline in mucopolysaccharidosis type I.
papers.summary: In a single patient with attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis type I and progressive cognitive decline, 24 months of intrathecal recombinant human α-L-iduronidase was associated with improved memory, adaptive functioning, school performance, white-matter integrity, and white-matter and corpus-callosum volume. Gray-matter and hippocampal volumes decreased, and treatment was tolerated with no serious adverse events, but the uncontrolled single-case design limits causal and generalizable conclusions.
papers.why: A patient with attenuated MPS I showed cognitive, school-performance, and white-matter MRI improvements after intrathecal IDUA delivered past the blood-brain barrier.

papers.title: Molecular Genetics and Metabolism Report Long-term follow-up of post hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for Hurler syndrome: clinical, biochemical, and pathological improvements.
papers.summary: In one 15-year-old male with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I who received hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at 2 years, long-term follow-up showed preserved cognition and activities of daily living, reduced blood dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, and improved bone histopathology. Skeletal deformity and abnormalities requiring surgery persisted, indicating incomplete skeletal remission, while blood keratan sulfate remained elevated and was proposed as a marker of skeletal dysplasia.
papers.why: Long-term follow-up after early HSCT documents clinical, biochemical, and pathological improvement in severe MPS I, including use of GAG levels and skeletal histology as outcomes.

papers.title: Targeting a Pre-existing Anti-transgene T Cell Response for Effective Gene Therapy of MPS-I in the Mouse Model of the Disease.
papers.summary: In pre-immunized idua−/− mice, pre-existing IDUA-specific CD8+ T cells selectively eliminated LV.IDUA-transduced HSCs and prevented their engraftment, whereas anti-IDUA IgG did not impair engraftment. CD8+ or T-cell depletion improved engraftment, with anti-CD3 producing profound depletion and more complete rescue than fludarabine, motivating monitoring and lymphodepleting conditioning in patients previously exposed to IDUA.
papers.why: Reports a strategy to overcome pre-existing anti-transgene T-cell responses and restore engraftment of IDUA-corrected hematopoietic cells in MPS I mice.

papers.title: Long term follow-up after haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for mucopolysaccharidosis type I-H: a retrospective study of 51 patients.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 51 patients with mucopolysaccharidosis type I-H, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation was associated with long-term survival, preserved or improved neurocognitive development, and normal leukocyte α-L-Iduronidase activity in many patients. Outcomes remained limited by transplant-related mortality and progressive skeletal, visual, hearing, airway, and cardiac complications, while enzyme replacement therapy improved soft-tissue and obstructive sleep apnea manifestations but had less effect on skeletal and cardiovascular disease.
papers.why: This 51-patient longitudinal study provides direct long-term efficacy, safety, neurodevelopmental, and functional outcome data for HSCT in MPS I-H.

papers.title: Long-term cognitive and somatic outcomes of enzyme replacement therapy in untransplanted Hurler syndrome.
papers.summary: This case report describes a 16-year-old patient with mucopolysaccharidosis type IH (Hurler syndrome) treated from age 27 months with weekly intravenous enzyme replacement therapy alone. Early ERT was associated with prolonged survival, a 62% reduction in urinary glycosaminoglycans, reduced organomegaly, and delayed neurocognitive deterioration, but hydrocephalus, spinal cord compression, corneal clouding, hearing loss, pain, stiffness, and other disease manifestations persisted or progressed; because this was a single uncontrolled case, causal CNS benefit and the effects of the higher dose remain uncertain.
papers.why: Reports long-term clinical outcomes of ERT monotherapy in Hurler syndrome, including preserved cognition and evolving systemic disease manifestations.

papers.title: Growth patterns for untreated individuals with MPS I: Report from the international MPS I registry.
papers.summary: This observational registry study constructs sex- and age-specific length/height and head-circumference reference curves for untreated individuals with severe and attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis type I. Severe MPS I is associated with early overgrowth followed by height below the third percentile by age 4, while untreated attenuated MPS I height falls below the third percentile by age 9; severe disease also shows persistently increased head circumference through age 3.
papers.why: Constructs disease-specific untreated growth reference curves from 670 registry individuals to support outcome evaluation and clinical monitoring.

papers.title: Intravenous delivery for treatment of mucopolysaccharidosis type I: A comparison of AAV serotypes 9 and rh10.
papers.summary: A single intravenous dose of AAV9-IDUA or AAVrh10-IDUA produced supraphysiological IDUA activity throughout peripheral tissues and the central nervous system in adult IDUA-deficient mice. Both vectors reduced urinary and tissue glycosaminoglycan storage, but CNS transduction appeared largely vascular, brain glycosaminoglycan reduction was incomplete in several regions, and the two serotypes showed no significant therapeutic differences.
papers.why: In MPS I mice, both AAV9 and AAVrh10 vectors produced widespread systemic and CNS IDUA expression and normalized tissue and urinary GAG accumulation.

papers.title: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell Derivation and Ex Vivo Gene Correction Using a Mucopolysaccharidosis Type 1 Disease Mouse Model.
papers.summary: The study demonstrates that Idua-deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts can be reprogrammed into pluripotent induced pluripotent stem cells and corrected by removal of a disruptive Neor cassette using CRISPR/Cas9. Gene-corrected cells retained pluripotency and recovered IDUA activity equivalent to wild-type cells after fibroblast and spontaneous differentiation, but editing efficiency was low and clinical safety was not established.
papers.why: The study demonstrates correction of an IDUA mutation in MPS I iPSCs using CRISPR/Cas9 and restores enzyme function to wild-type levels.

papers.title: Decreased performance in IDUA knockout mouse mimic limitations of joint function and locomotion in patients with Hurler syndrome.
papers.summary: The study generated an IDUA knockout mouse model with a large deletion spanning parts of exons 6–9 and showed increased urinary and tissue glycosaminoglycan accumulation, increased bone mineral density, and reduced grip strength, rotarod performance, and open-field activity. These behavioral abnormalities mimic the joint-mobility and locomotor limitations reported in patients with mucopolysaccharidosis type I, supporting the model for studying disease mechanisms and therapeutic approaches.
papers.why: This study provides an IDUA-deficient mouse model with behavioral, biochemical, bone, joint, and locomotor measures that reproduce key MPS I phenotypes.

papers.title: Airway Abnormalities in Adult Mucopolysaccharidosis and Development of Salford Mucopolysaccharidosis Airway Score.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 31 adults with mucopolysaccharidosis, airway abnormalities were common and multidimensional, while the MPS I patients had comparatively milder abnormalities. The paper proposes the Salford Mucopolysaccharidosis Airway Score (SMAS) to quantify airway severity, with scores above 25 suggesting a difficult airway, but acknowledges the need for larger multicenter validation.
papers.why: The study develops and clinically evaluates an airway severity score in a cohort that includes MPS I patients and identifies thresholds for airway intervention and difficult-airway prediction.

papers.title: An engineered U7 small nuclear RNA scaffold greatly increases ADAR-mediated programmable RNA base editing.
papers.summary: The paper shows that an engineered SmOPT U7 antisense RNA scaffold markedly improves endogenous-ADAR-mediated A-to-G editing from a single genetic copy. In the IDUA-W392X mouse model of Hurler syndrome, a single systemic AAV PHP.eB injection produced 75% target editing in anterior cerebral cortex, restored IDUA enzyme activity, and reduced glycosaminoglycan accumulation to wild-type levels, although Idua transcript abundance remained low.
papers.why: The engineered U7 scaffold achieved high ADAR-mediated RNA editing in vitro and 75% editing in Hurler syndrome mouse brain after systemic AAV delivery.

papers.title: Liver-Directed Human Amniotic Epithelial Cell Transplantation Improves Systemic Disease Phenotype in Hurler Syndrome Mouse Model.
papers.summary: In an Idua-null mouse model of mucopolysaccharidosis type 1, two liver-directed injections of unfractionated human amniotic epithelial cells restored hepatic IDUA activity, reduced urinary glycosaminoglycan excretion, and improved craniofacial bone, joint, and sensorimotor phenotypes for up to 28 weeks. The treatment did not significantly restore IDUA activity outside the liver or markedly improve sampled liver histology, and residual skeletal abnormalities remained.
papers.why: This preclinical study demonstrates that liver-directed human amniotic epithelial-cell transplantation restores IDUA activity and improves systemic, skeletal, and neurologic phenotypes in an MPS I mouse model.

papers.title: Report of Five Years of Experience in Neonatal Screening for Mucopolysaccharidosis Type I and Review of the Literature.
papers.summary: In a five-year newborn-screening program, sequential measurement of IDUA activity followed by glycosaminoglycan analysis in dried blood spots identified two newborns with MPS I and eliminated false-positive referrals caused by IDUA pseudodeficiency during the final 18 months. Both affected children received early laronidase-based enzyme replacement therapy, and the child with a severe Hurler phenotype also underwent unrelated cord-blood hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; both had favorable clinical outcomes at follow-up, although persistent corneal clouding or skeletal and facial abnormalities remained.
papers.why: This MPS I screening program validates IDUA activity measurement with GAG second-tier testing for reducing pseudodeficiency false positives and enabling early treatment.

papers.title: A rapid and non-invasive proteomic analysis using DBS and buccal swab for multiplexed second-tier screening of Pompe disease and Mucopolysaccharidosis type I.
papers.summary: The paper demonstrates a multiplexed Immuno-SRM assay that directly quantifies endogenous IDUA protein in dried blood spots and buccal swabs for second-tier screening of MPS I. IDUA was undetectable in severe and moderate naïve cases and markedly reduced in attenuated cases, but the small cohorts, carrier overlap, uncertain variants, and lack of prospective cutoff validation limit diagnostic performance and treatment monitoring claims.
papers.why: The study develops and clinically evaluates a rapid proteomic assay that distinguishes severe and attenuated MPS I from pseudodeficiency and carrier states.

papers.title: An At-Risk Population Screening Program for Mucopolysaccharidoses by Measuring Urinary Glycosaminoglycans in Taiwan.
papers.summary: The study established a prospective at-risk screening program in which urinary dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, and keratan sulfate were quantified by LC-MS/MS and followed by leukocyte enzyme activity and genetic testing for confirmation. Among 13 children diagnosed with mucopolysaccharidosis, including three with MPS I, LC-MS/MS fraction biomarkers had no observed false negatives, whereas the urinary DMB/creatinine ratio had a 31% false-negative rate across the MPS cohort.
papers.why: Reports a validated urinary GAG LC-MS/MS screening algorithm that successfully detected MPS I and other MPS subtypes in an at-risk pediatric population.

papers.title: Nucleoside analogs in ADAR guide strands targeting 5'-UA̲ sites.
papers.summary: The study identifies guide-RNA nucleoside analogs that increase or inhibit ADAR-mediated adenosine-to-inosine editing. For the mouse IDUA W392X model of Hurler syndrome, 2′-deoxynebularine (dN) at the guide −1 position increased deamination by both ADAR1 and ADAR2, whereas sequence-dependent effects were observed for other analogs; editing and therapeutic rescue in MPS I patients were not tested.
papers.why: The study directly tests nucleoside-modified guide RNAs for ADAR editing and reports enhanced editing at a mouse IDUA W392X nonsense site, providing a potentially transferable therapeutic method for IDUA mutations.

papers.title: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I: molecular characteristics of two novel alpha-L-iduronidase mutations in Tunisian patients.
papers.summary: Sequencing six unrelated Tunisian families identified four homozygous IDUA variants associated with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I, including the novel p.F177S missense variant and p.L530fs insertion frameshift. Enzymatic testing showed deficient or undetectable IDUA activity, and the findings support mutation analysis for carrier detection, genotype–phenotype assessment, and prenatal diagnosis in these families.
papers.why: Reports targeted IDUA sequencing that identified causal and novel variants and supports molecular diagnosis and counselling in MPS I.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of YW17 (Laronidase-CinnaGen) Compared to Aldurazyme® in MPS I Patients
papers.summary:
The purpose of this phase III study is to assess the efficacy and safety of YW17 produced by CinnaGen Company compared to Aldurazyme® in mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I) patients.

All patients receive Aldurazyme® for 12 weeks, followed by YW17 for another 12 weeks.

The primary outcome is the assessment of the maintenance of the mean uGAG levels at the end of each medication administration. The secondary outcomes are the assessment of 6-minute walking test (6MWT), predicted forced vital capacity (FVC), enzyme activity assay, and adverse events (AEs).

papers.title: A Study Evaluating the Safety and Pharmacokinetics of Aldurazyme® (Laronidase) in MPS I Patients Less Than 5 Years Old
papers.summary: The main objectives of this study are to evaluate the safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) of enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant human alpha-L-iduronidase \[Aldurazyme® (laronidase)\] in mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I) patients less than 5 years old. Efficacy measurements will also be evaluated in this study.

papers.title: A Study of the Effect of Aldurazyme® (Laronidase) Treatment on Lactation in Female Patients With Mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I) and Their Breastfed Infants
papers.summary: The purpose of this study is to determine if laronidase is present in the breast milk of post-partum women receiving Aldurazyme® (laronidase) and the effects of Aldurazyme (laronidase) on the growth, development, and immunologic response of their breastfed infants.

papers.title: Study of Aldurazyme® Replacement Therapy in Patients With Mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I) Disease
papers.summary:
This is a multi-center, open label, study conducted to evaluate the safety of laronidase administered by intravenous drip infusion in Japanese patients with MPS I disease.

Following baseline evaluation, patients will receive weekly infusions of JC0498 at an intravenous dose of 100 units/kg. Patient safety will be monitored continuously throughout the trial. In addition, the effects of JC0498 treatment in this patient population will be assessed by periodically evaluating aspects of MPS I disease in patients at scheduled intervals over the duration of the trial.
